ety: From Middle English, borrowed from Old French fable, from Latin fābula, from fārī (“to speak, say”) + -bula (“instrumental suffix”). See ban, and compare fabulous, fame. Doublet of fabula.

s.def: A fictitious narrative intended to enforce some useful truth or precept, usually with animals, etc. as characters; an apologue. Prototypically, Aesop's Fables.
Any story told to excite wonder; common talk; the theme of talk.
ex: […]we grew / The fable of the city where we dwelt.

s.def: Fiction; untruth; falsehood.
ex: I say it would look like a fable to report that this gentleman gives away all which is the overplus of a great fortune by secret methods to other men.

s.def: The plot, story, or connected series of events forming the subject of an epic or dramatic poem.

ety: Borrowed from French fabrique, from Latin fabrica (“a workshop, art, trade, product of art, structure, fabric”), from faber (“artisan, workman”). Doublet of fabrica, borrowed from Latin, and forge, borrowed from Old French.

ety: From Middle English fabricaten (“to fashion, make”), from Latin fabricātus, perfect active participle of fabricor (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fabrica (“a fabric, building”) + -or (verb-forming suffix); see fabric and forge. Cognate with French fabriquer.

ex: You are all resolved rather to die than to famish?

s.def: To suffer extremity from deprivation of anything essential or necessary.
ex: The Lord will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish.

ety: From Middle English famous, from Anglo-Norman famous, from Latin fāmōsus, equivalent to fame + -ous. Displaced native Old English hlīsful.

s.def: Well known.
In the public eye.
ex: Some people are only famous within their city.

s.def: Excellent.
ex: Pagett is a famous Job's comforter.

s.def: To make famous; to bring renown to.

ety: From Latin famulus (“servant”).

s.def: A close attendant or assistant, especially of a magician or occult scholar.

ety: Inherited from Middle English fan, inherited from Old English fann (“a winnowing, fan”), derived from Latin vannus (“fan for winnowing grain”), derived from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”). Cognates * Latin ventus (“wind”) * Dutch wan (“winnowing basket”) * German Wanne (“winnowing basket”) * Swedish vanna (“a fan for winnowing”) * Old English windwian (“to fan, winnow”). More at winnow.

s.def: A hand-held device consisting of concertinaed material, or slats of material, gathered together at one end, that may be opened out into the shape of a sector of a circle and waved back and forth in order to move air towards oneself and cool oneself.
An electrical or mechanical device for moving air, used for cooling people, machinery, etc.
ex: He didn't switch on the fan because the temperature was 15 degrees Celsius.

s.def: To blow air on (something) by means of a fan (hand-held, mechanical or electrical) or otherwise.
ex: We enjoyed standing at the edge of the cliff, being fanned by the wind.
Alice took up the fan and gloves, and, as the hall was very hot, she kept fanning herself all the time she went on talking: […]

s.def: A person who is fond of something or someone, especially an admirer of a performer or aficionado of a sport.
ex: I am a big fan of libraries.
I am a big fan of cricket.

s.def: The action of fanning; agitation of the air.
ex: "If I cannot be of service, then I certainly don't wish to impose," said McGinty, with a quick fan of breeze that indicated a sweeping bow.

s.def: Anything resembling a hand-held fan in shape, e.g., a peacock’s tail.
An instrument for winnowing grain, by moving which the grain is tossed and agitated, and the chaff is separated and blown away.
A small vane or sail, used to keep the large sails of a smock mill always in the direction of the wind.
A group of overlapping cards exposed in various patience games.
A section of a tree having a finite number of branches.

ety: First attested in 1525. Learned borrowing from Latin fānāticus (“of a temple, divinely inspired, frenzied”), from fānum (“temple”). Influenced by French fanatique.

s.def: Fanatical.
ex: But Faith, fanatic Faith, once wedded fast / To some dear falsehood, hugs it to the last.

s.def: Showing evidence of possession by a god or demon; frenzied, overzealous.
A person who is zealously enthusiastic for some cause.
ex: A zealot can't change his mind. A fanatic can't change his mind and won't change the subject. —Winston Churchill (attributed)
A fanatic is one who redoubles his effort when he has forgotten his aim. —George Santayana

s.def: Having an extreme, irrational zeal or enthusiasm for a specific cause.
ex: fanatical devotion
fanatical belief
fanatical follower

ety: From fan + belt.

s.def: A belt which turns a cooling fan in a car engine.

ety: From fancy (“to have a fancy for, like; to imagine, suppose”) + -ed.

ex: Near-synonyms: conceptual, fanciful, ideal, notional
The plant was named for its fancied resemblance to a Roman spear.
[S]till by the maid / Love went submiss, with eye more dangerous / Than fancied basilisk to wound whoe'er / Too bold approached, […]

s.def: Organized, or (especially of attire) designed, to suit one's fancy or whim.
Having a fancy (“inclination, liking, or love”) for; desired, favourite.
ex: The visitors were worthy winners, taking the game to the highly fancied hosts from the first minute.

s.def: Predicted to win or succeed.
ex: the fancied team in the tournament

s.def: Designed in an artistic manner.
ex: His seals are curiously fancied, and exquisitely well cut, and of great use to encourage young gentlemen to write a good hand.

s.def: simple past and past participle of fancy

ety: From fancy (verb) + -er.

s.def: One who fancies; a person with a special interest, attraction or liking for something.
ex: She's definitely a cat fancier: she has nine of them in her home and the walls are covered with pictures of more.
Even so, most lily fanciers would rather have a colony of goldbands than any other species or hybrids in existence.

s.def: A person who breeds or grows a particular animal or plant for points of excellence.
One who fancies or imagines.
comparative form of fancy: more fancy

ety: From fancy + -ful.

s.def: Imaginative or fantastic; ignoring reality.
ex: Near-synonyms: conceptual, fancied, ideal, notional
It was fanciful to suppose that all he had to do would be to stride into a top law firm and he would be hired on the spot.

s.def: Unreal or imagined.

ety: From Middle English fansy, fantsy, a contraction of fantasy, fantasye, fantasie, from Old French fantasie, from Medieval Latin fantasia, from Late Latin phantasia (“an idea, notion, fancy, phantasm”), from Ancient Greek φαντασία (phantasía), from φαντάζω (phantázō, “to render visible”), from φαντός (phantós, “visible”), from φαίνω (phaínō, “to make visible”); from the same root as φάος (pháos, “light”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰh₂nyéti, from the root *bʰeh₂- (“to shine”). Doublet…

s.def: The imagination.
ex: […] But know that in the soul / Are many lesser faculties, that serve / Reason as chief; among these Fancy next / Her office holds […]
In the Spring a livelier iris changes on the burnish’d dove; / In the Spring a young man’s fancy lightly turns to thoughts of love.
For a time she could not soothe nor convince him that it was fancy.

s.def: An image or representation of anything formed in the mind.
An opinion or notion formed without much reflection.
ex: I have always had a Fancy, that Learning might be made a Play and Recreation to Children […]
I dare say I am merely a foolish woman with a young girl's fancies.

s.def: A whim.
ex: I had a fancy to learn to play the flute.

s.def: Love or amorous attachment.
ex: And they’ve taken a fancy to me, Aunt said. Kitto and the others. That means they like me.

s.def: Liking.
ex: He took a fancy to the goods in the window.

s.def: The object of inclination or liking.
ex: For you, fair Hermia, look you arm yourself / To fit your fancies to your father’s will;

s.def: Any sport or hobby pursued by a group.
ex: Trainspotting is the fancy of a special lot.
the cat fancy

s.def: The enthusiasts of such a pursuit.
ex: He fell out of favor with the boxing fancy after the incident.

s.def: A diamond with a distinctive colour.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish fandango, of uncertain origin. Possibly related to Portuguese fado, or of West African origin.

s.def: A form of lively flamenco music and dance that has many regional variations (e.g. fandango de Huelva), some of which have their own names (e.g. malagueña, granadina).
ex: We skipped the light fandango / Turned cartwheels 'cross the floor
I see a little silhouetto of a man / Scaramouche, Scaramouche, will you do the fandango?
I'm wearing a Spanish skirt so what's wrong with dancing a fandango.

s.def: A gathering for dancing; a ball.
ex: When Auguste Fretéllière and the painter Theodore Gentilz attended a fandango in the 1840s, the festivities took place near Military Plaza.

s.def: An unknown entity or contraption.
ex: What’s that fandango you’re using?
She had on a new silk dress, flounced clear up to her knees, and some kind of a fandango of a thing on her shoulders.

s.def: A confusion; a chaotic collection.
ex: A splotch of colour on a wall charmed his eye, a fandango of shadows, the nonchalant pose of some labourer.
Such a fandango of wicked lies Mrs. Love had never heard tell in all her born days.

s.def: An extravaganza; an instance of lavish and fantastical events or behavior.
ex: Scaramouche, what a fandango of a life.

s.def: A shade of red-violet.
Vagina.
ex: So, what? She strangled her and stuck a broken bottle up her... fandango?

s.def: To dance the fandango.
To dance, particularly with a lot of energy.

ety: From Middle English fane, from Old English fana (“cloth, banner”), from Proto-West Germanic *fanō, from Proto-Germanic *fanô (“cloth, flag”), from Proto-Indo-European *peh₂n- (“to weave; something woven; cloth, fabric, tissue”). Doublet of fanon and vane.

s.def: A weathercock, a weather vane.
A banner, especially a military banner.
A temple or sacred place.
ex: Fanes are built around it for a distance of 3, 4 or 5 Indian miles; but whether these are Jaina, or more strictly Hindu is not mentioned.
It was a wonderful sight to see the full moon looking down on the ruined fane of Kør.

ety: Borrowed from French fanfare; some senses apparently influenced by surface analysis, fan + fare.

s.def: A flourish of trumpets or horns as to announce; a short and lively air performed on hunting horns during the chase.
ex: They played a short fanfare to announce the arrival of the king.
This new locomotive was turned out of Doncaster works in May, 1934, to a mighty fanfare of trumpets.

s.def: A show of ceremony or celebration.
ex: The town opened the new library with fanfare and a speech from the mayor.

s.def: To play a fanfare.
ex: At this the trumpeters again most earnestly fanfared,
The miscreant is shamed into just standing there mortified and not fanfaring at all while the others finish the greeting to the arriving guest.
A hundred trumpets fanfared as they entered, echoing brazenly in the black vault above.

s.def: To embellish with fanfares.
ex: PAM is a guitar song fanfared by massive chords on an acoustic 12-string (probably (ribbed From The Who's contemporary hit 'Pinball Wizard').

s.def: To imitate a fanfare, in order to dramatize the presentation or introduction of something.
ex: The name of the farm we were staying on was, tun-tun-tah,' I fanfared dramatically, 'Le Tomple, the temple. Spooky eh?'
'Ta-ra!' fan-fared Jackie, showing off her dress.

s.def: To introduce with pomp and show.
ex: Cohorts of charabancs fanfared Offa's province and his concern, negotiating the by-ways from Teme to Trent.
It could be fêted and fanfared and ushered into the white-tie events with a guest pass that read Literature with a capital 'L'.

s.def: To mark an arrival or departure with music, noise, or drama.
ex: The daffodils I planted in the autumn are marching their way along the path, strident trumpets fanfaring the first warmish day of the year.

s.def: To publicize or announce.
ex: So, did quacks cash in on this, fanfaring their own capacity to quell pain?
It was fanfared as 'hello, 1964' and advertised as 'the place billionaires goto get away from millionaires'.

s.def: To fan out.
ex: Just so, light beaded on tin lanterns, drops fanfared from sprinklers, minnows fluted in pools.
These autumn flowers were in full bloom, fanfaring in the cool autumn wind.

ety: From French fanfaronnade (“bragging, boasting”); other senses influenced by fanfare.

s.def: Empty, self-assertive boasting; an instance of such behaviour.
Loud, showy display, celebration or proclamation (of something), sometimes involving the playing of trumpets or other musical instruments.
ex: With a fanfaronade of welcome they lowered their drawbridges
[…] we sailed gracefully out of the hotel yard, Rattray too- tooing a fanfaronade on the horn.
Mrs. Burnside indicated her disapproval of all this with a fanfaronade of flatulence.

s.def: To engage in empty, self-assertive boasting.
To proclaim loudly; to promote enthusiastically.
ex: […] I criticised her straight Teutonic fringe and fanfaronaded on the captivating frizziness of Joanna’s hair.

s.def: To make a noisy, showy display or celebration; to play a fanfare.

ety: From clipping of fangtooth, from Middle English *fangtooth, *fengtooth, from Old English fengtōþ (“molar tooth”), from feng, preterite of fōn (“to catch, take, seize”). a tooth that can inject venom

Synonym of tooth, particularly in humans.

ex: Is not this something more than fantasy?
A thousand fantasies / Begin to throng into my memory.

s.def: The drug gamma-hydroxybutyric acid.

s.def: A document that details how to play and win a video game; a strategy guide.

ex: They are on the far right on this issue.

ex: Is there not a far difference between asking it up and urging it, Mr. Secretary?

ety: Borrowed from Middle French farce (“farce (style of humor); stuffing”) (in the latter sense, via Middle English fars, farsse), from Old French farse, from Medieval Latin farsa, from the feminine perfect passive participle of Latin farciō (“to stuff”). s.def: A style of humor marked by broad improbabilities with little regard to regularity or method.
A motion picture or play featuring this style of humor.
ex: The farce that we saw last night had us laughing and shaking our heads at the same time.

s.def: A situation abounding with ludicrous incidents.
ex: The first month of labor negotiations was a farce.

s.def: A ridiculous or empty show.

ety: From flag + pole.

s.def: A tall pole up which one or more flags may be raised and flown.

ety: From Middle French flagrant, from Latin flagrantem, present participle of flagrare (“blaze, burn”). More at black.

ety: From flag + ship.

To move like a flail.

ety: From Middle English flayre, from Old French flair (“scent, odour”), from flairier (“to reek, smell”), from Latin flāgrō, dissimilated variation of frāgrō (“emit a sweet smell”, verb). More at fragrant.

ex: to have a flair for art

ety: Borrowed from German FlaK, short for Fliegerabwehrkanone (“anti airplane cannon”).

ety: From Middle English flake (“a flake of snow”), from Old English flacca and/or Old Norse flak (“loose or torn piece”) (compare Old Norse flakna (“to flake or chip”)), from Proto-Germanic *flaką (“something flat”), from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂- (“flat, broad, plain”). ety: 17th century; from flim-flam, itself perhaps from a dialectal word or Scandinavian; compare Old Norse flim (“lampoon, mockery”).

ety: Borrowed from French flamboyant (“flaming, wavy”), participle of flamboyer (“to flame”), from Old French flamboier, from flambe (“flame”). The architectural style derives its name from the flame-like shapes in the tracery.

ety: From Middle English flawme, blend of Old French flame and flambe, flamble, the first from Latin flamma, the second from Latin flammula, diminutive of flamma, both from pre-Latin *fladma; Proto-Italic *flagmā, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰel- (“to shimmer, gleam, shine”). ety: Origin uncertain, first recorded in the mid 16th century, probably related to Latin flagrō (“to burn”). ety: In some senses, from Middle English flasshen, a variant of flasken, flaskien (“to sprinkle, splash”), which was likely of imitative origin; in other senses probably of North Germanic origin akin to Swedish dialectal flasa (“to burn brightly, blaze”), related to flare. ety: From the days of flintlock firearms, where the main charge was intended to be fired by a small charge of gunpowder in the flash pan. ety: From Anglo-Norman floteson, from Old French flotaison (“a floating”), from floter (“to float”), of Germanic origin (See float.), + -aison, from Latin -atio.

s.def: Debris floating in a river or sea, in particular fragments from a shipwreck.
ex: STORAGE boxes -- catchalls for flotsam, jetsam, whatnots and thingamajigs -- are gaining new interest as decorative objects for the home.
“What about that one?” “That'll do nicely. That gaggle of human flotsam doesn't even belong on the sea.”

ety: Probably of North Germanic origin, from Norwegian flunsa (“hurry”), perhaps ultimately imitative. Or, perhaps formed on the pattern of pounce, bounce.

s.def: To move in a bouncy, exaggerated manner.
To depart in a dramatic, haughty way that draws attention to oneself.
ex: After failing to win the leadership election, he flounced dramatically.
'Oh certainly,' retorted Tinette impudently, as she flounced out of the room.
You got your ass kicked and instead of admitting you might have made a mistake, you flounced.

s.def: To flounder; to make spastic motions.
ex: To flutter and flounce will do nothing but batter and bruise us.
With his broad fins and forky tail he laves / The rising surge, and flounces in the waves.

s.def: To decorate with a flounce.
A strip of decorative material, usually pleated, attached along one edge; a ruffle.
ex: Then he looked from her to some gayer figures moving along the road with flutters of bright streamers and flounces

s.def: The act of flouncing; a dramatic departure.
A row of corrugations, skin folds, or spines, on the hemipenis of a snake.

ety: From Middle English flowndre, from Anglo-Norman floundre, from Old Northern French flondre, from Old Norse flyðra, from Proto-Germanic *flunþrijǭ. Cognate with Danish flynder, German Flunder, Swedish flundra.

s.def: A European species of flatfish having dull brown colouring with reddish-brown blotches; fluke, European flounder (Platichthys flesus).
Any of various flatfish of the family Pleuronectidae or Bothidae.
A bootmaker's tool for crimping boot fronts.
To act clumsily or confused; to struggle or be flustered.
ex: He gave a good speech, but floundered when audience members asked questions he could not answer well.
They have floundered on from blunder to blunder.
These epics nearly always had runaway trains, nincompoops floundering with the controls and a collapsed bridge just ahead!

s.def: To flop around as a fish out of water.
To make clumsy attempts to move or regain one's balance.
ex: Robert yanked Connie's leg vigorously, causing her to flounder and eventually fall.

s.def: To be in serious difficulty.

ety: Spelled (until about 1830) and meaning flower in the sense of flour being the "finest portion of ground grain" (compare French fleur de farine, fine fleur). Doublet of fleur, flor, and flower. Partially displaced native meal. The U.S. standard of identity comes from 21CFR137.105.

s.def: Powder obtained by grinding or milling cereal grains, especially wheat, or other foodstuffs such as soybeans and potatoes, and used to bake bread, cakes, and pastry.

The food made by grinding and bolting cleaned wheat (not durum or red durum) until it meets specified levels of fineness, dryness, and freedom from bran and germ, also containing any of certain enzymes, ascorbic acid, and certain bleaching agents.
Powder of other material.
ex: mustard flour

s.def: Obsolete form of flower.
ex: that nobody is wished to see my dead body. & that no murnurs walk behind me at my funeral. & that no flours be planted on my grave.

s.def: To apply flour to something; to cover with flour.
ex: Flour the surface before rolling out the dough.

s.def: To reduce to flour.
To break up into fine globules of mercury in the amalgamation process.
flour-feeding moth of the family Pyralidae
Any of several small moths of the Pyralidae family whose larvae feed on flour.

ety: From flour + monger. Compare the Middle English surname Flurmongester.

s.def: A seller of flour.
ex: […]I heard a ruffian behind saying, “E un farinajuolo” (“He is a meal-monger,” or rather “flour-monger”).
Finally, the department of agriculture maintains practically a year-round surveillance to keep the bread-flour mongers from their greedy grabs.
“You first,” he said sharply, pointing at the flour-monger.

ety: From Middle English floryschen, from Old French florir (via the arrhizotonic stem floriss-), from Late Latin flōrīre, from Latin flōrēre, from Latin flōrem (“flower”, noun). Corresponds to flower + -ish.

s.def: To thrive or grow well.
ex: The barley flourished in the warm weather.

s.def: To prosper or fare well.
ex: The town flourished with the coming of the railway.
The cooperation flourished as the customers rushed in the business.
Bad men as frequently prosper and flourish, and that by the means of their wickedness.

s.def: To be in a period of greatest influence.
ex: His writing flourished before the war.

s.def: To develop; to make thrive; to expand.
To make bold, sweeping movements with.
ex: They flourished the banner as they stormed the palace.
The squirrel flourished its fluffy tail about as an alarm signal after its narrow escape from the cat.

s.def: To make bold and sweeping, fanciful, or wanton movements, by way of ornament, parade, bravado, etc.; to play with fantastic and irregular motion.
ex: Impetuous spread the stream, and smoking flourished o'er his head.

s.def: To use florid language; to indulge in rhetorical figures and lofty expressions.
ex: They dilate […] and flourish long upon little incidents.

s.def: To make ornamental strokes with the pen; to write graceful, decorative figures.
To adorn with beautiful figures or rhetoric; to ornament with anything showy; to embellish.
ex: With shadowy verdure flourish'd high, A sudden youth the groves enjoy.

s.def: To execute an irregular or fanciful strain of music, by way of ornament or prelude.
ex: Why do the emperor's trumpets flourish thus?

ety: From Middle English floury, equivalent to flour + -y. Piecewise doublet of flowery.

s.def: Resembling flour.
ex: These mashed potatoes have a floury texture.

s.def: Covered in flour.
ex: The baker wiped his floury hands on his apron.

s.def: High in starch; tending to break down easily when cooked.
ex: Boil four large floury potatoes till they are thoroughly done; peel them and mash them smooth with the back of a spoon

ety: Perhaps from Middle English flouten (“to play the flute”); compare with Dutch fluiten.

s.def: To express contempt for (laws, rules, etc.) by word or action.
ex: The manoeuvres of Microsoft and HP appear to comply with the letter of the regulations, even if they flout their spirit.

s.def: To scorn.
ex: Yet all ' s not worth a pin, But could not get her; Phillida flouts me. Dick had her to the Vine
Three gaudy standards flout the pale blue sky.

s.def: The act by which something is flouted; violation of a law.
ex: A flout is when someone deliberately and ostentatiously contravenes a maxim.

s.def: A mockery or insult.

ety: From Middle English flowe, from the verb (see below). The psychology sense “state of focus” was coined by Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi in 1975.

s.def: The rising movement of the tide.
the movement of a fluid
To move as a fluid from one position to another.
ex: Rivers flow from springs and lakes.
Tears flow from the eyes.
Wrex: I need to get my blood flowing. Find me something to kill!

s.def: Movement in people or things characterized with a continuous motion, involving either a non solid mass or a multitude.
The movement of a real or figurative fluid.
A formalization of the idea of the motion of particles in a fluid, as a group action of the real numbers on a set.
ex: The notion of flow is basic to the study of ordinary differential equations.

s.def: Smoothness or continuity.
ex: The room was small, but it had good symmetry and flow.

s.def: The amount of a fluid that moves or the rate of fluid movement.
ex: Turn on the valve and make sure you have sufficient flow.
Other devices measure water flow in streams fed by melted ice.

s.def: A flow pipe, carrying liquid away from a boiler or other central plant (compare with return pipe which returns fluid to central plant).
A mental state characterized by concentration, focus, and enjoyment of a given task.
A schematic representation of how the different stages in a process are interconnected.

ety: From Middle English flour, from Anglo-Norman flur, from Latin flōrem, accusative of flōs, from Proto-Italic *flōs, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰleh₃- (“to thrive, bloom”). Doublet of fleur, flor, flour, bloom, and blossom. Partly displaced native Old English blostma (which is cognate), whence Modern English blossom.

s.def: A reproductive structure in angiosperms (flowering plants), often conspicuously colourful and typically including sepals, petals, and either or both stamens and/or a pistil.
To put forth blooms.
ex: This plant flowers in June.

s.def: A colorful, conspicuous structure associated with angiosperms, frequently scented and attracting various insects, and which may or may not be used for sexual reproduction.
ex: The flowers glowed red and golden: snapdragons and sunflowers, and nasturtians trailing all over the turf walls and peeping in at the round windows.

s.def: A plant that bears flowers, especially a plant that is small and lacks wood.
ex: We transplanted the flowers to a larger pot.

s.def: The stem of a flowering plant with the blossom or blossoms attached, used for decoration, as a gift, etc.
ex: He always keeps a vase full of flowers in his office.

s.def: Of plants, a state of bearing blooms.
ex: The dogwoods are in flower this week.

s.def: The vulva, especially the labia majora.

ety: From flower + pot.

ety: From Middle English floury, equivalent to flower + -y (adjectival suffix). Piecewise doublet of floury.

s.def: Pertaining to or characteristic of flowers.
Decorated with or abundant in flowers.

Melodramatic, overexaggerated.
ex: He kissed her hand in a way she found just a little flowery.

s.def: Someone or something considered flowery.
ex: It was well done up to that point -- apart from a few sneaky attacks of the floweries.

s.def: Diminutive of flower.
ex: Hearken these blissful birdies how they sing, / And see the freshé floweries, how they spring!”
That pottie’s too wee for six, Minnie, lassie. Go ben to the room press and you’ll see a big brown one with blue floweries on it.
I wore a white dress with yellow, grey and black floweries on it and a large white hat.

transmit flu

ety: First attested in 1630; borrowed from Latin flūctuātus, perfect passive participle of flūctuō (“(of the sea) to surge, swell; (of man) to waver, fluctuate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

To undulate.
To be irresolute; to waver.
ex: I fluctuated between wishing he was back home and wishing I'd never met him.

s.def: To cause to vary irregularly.
To rise and fall as a wave; to be tossed up and down the waves.
Tossed up and down the waves.
Wavering, fickle.

ety: Borrowed from Latin fluctuatiōnem, accusative singular of fluctuatiō, from fluctuō, from fluctus. Morphologically fluctuate + -ion.

ex: fluctuations of opinion
fluctuations of prices

ex: the fluctuations of the sea

ety: From Middle English flue, flewe (“mouthpiece of a hunting horn”), of uncertain origin. Alternatively, perhaps an alteration of Middle English floute, fleute, flote (“a pipe”), see English flute. Compare also Middle Dutch vloegh (“groove, channel, flute of a fluted column”).

s.def: A pipe or duct that carries gaseous combustion products away from the point of combustion (such as a furnace).
An enclosed passageway in which to direct a current of air or other gases along.
A woolly or downy substance; down, nap; a piece of this.
In an organ flue pipe, the opening between the lower lip and the languet.
Alternative form of flew (“shallow, flat”).

ety: From Late Latin fluentia, equivalent to fluent + -cy. Cognate with French fluence.

The inherent ability to use a language easily and accurately.

ety: From Latin fluens (“flowing”), present active participle of fluō (“to flow”).

Ah, fluff. My happy place. These fics are dedicated to feel-good feelings, which are the very best type of feelings.

ety: From fluff + -y. Compare German flauschig (“fluffy”).

ex: Fluffy bunny rabbits are really nice to stroke.

ety: Unknown, perhaps dialectal. It seems to have originally referred to a lucky shot at billiards. Possibly connected to sense 3, referring to whales' use of flukes to move rapidly. Possibly derived from German Glück (“luck, good fortune, happiness”).

It's Christmas at ground zero / Now the missiles are on their way / What a crazy fluke / We're gonna get nuked / On this jolly holiday

ex: After casting the bronze statue, we filed down the flukes and spurs from the molding process.

To shirk (a task or duty).
To back out through fear. (Commonly in the phrase 'flunk it', the 'it' referring to a specific task avoided; sometimes without specific reference, describing a person's attitude to life in general.)
A person who always agrees with their superior or employer.
One performing menial or miscellaneous duties.
Alternative form of flunkey.

ety: Perhaps an American English blend of flutter and hurry. Alternatively, perhaps from an obsolete term flurr (“scatter”).

s.def: A light, brief snowfall; a shower of snow.
A sudden and brief blast or gust; a light, temporary breeze.
ex: a flurry of wind

s.def: A shower of dust, leaves etc. brought on by a sudden gust of wind.
Any sudden activity; a stir.
ex: "I missed the beast in my flurry, but he dropped you all right and was off like a streak."
Higglety, pigglety, pop! The dog has eaten the mop; The pig's in a hurry, The cat's in a flurry, Higglety, pigglety, pop!

s.def: A snack consisting of soft ice cream mixed with small pieces of fruit, cookie crumbs, etc.

An occurrence of something (countable instances) in large numbers, happening suddenly or in a short period of time.
ex: The fencer landed a flurry of hits on her opponent.
The think piece provoked a flurry of media responses for the remainder of the week.

s.def: To agitate, bewilder, fluster.
ex: And so venturing not to say another word, poor Jemima trotted off, exceedingly flurried and nervous.

s.def: To move or fall in a flurry.

ety: From Middle English flusshen, fluschen, of uncertain origin. Compare dialectal flusk (“to fly at, startle a bird out of the bush”) and flusker (“to flutter, fly irregularly”). Perhaps related to Middle English flasshen, flasschen, flaschen, see flash; or a Middle English blend of flowen (“to flow”) + guschen (“to gush”). Compare Saterland Frisian flutskje, German Low German flutschen, German flutschen.

s.def: Smooth, even, aligned; not sticking out.
ex: Sand down the excess until it is flush with the surface.

s.def: Wealthy or well off.
ex: He just got a bonus so he's flush today.

s.def: Particularly, such a cleansing of a toilet.
Particularly, to cleanse a toilet by introducing a large amount of water.
To be cleansed by being flooded with generous quantities of water.

s.def: A group of birds that have suddenly started up from undergrowth, trees, etc.
To cause to take flight from concealment.
ex: The dogs flushed the deer from the woods.

s.def: To take suddenly to flight, especially from cover.
ex: A covey of quail flushed from the undergrowth.

s.def: Ellipsis of flush left and right: a body of text aligned with both its left and right margins.
Full of vigor; fresh; glowing; bright.
ex: With all his crimes broad blown, as flush as May.

s.def: A toilet that uses water to flush urine and feces through a pipe to another location, typically a sewer main in urban settings or a septic tank elsewhere.

ety: The verb is probably from Middle English *flostren (implied in flostring, flostrynge (“agitation; blustering”)) from a Scandinavian (North Germanic) language; compare Icelandic flaustra (“to bustle”), flaustr (“a bustle; a hurry”). Compare Old English flustrian (“to weave, plait, braid”). The noun is derived from the verb.

ex: The aged housekeeper was no less flustered and hurried in obeying the numerous and contradictory commands of her mistress, […]
Weel, Sam'l, I d'na want to fluster ye, but she's been ower lang wi' Lisbeth Fargus no to hae learnt her ways.

s.def: To make emotionally overwhelmed or visibly embarrassed, especially in a sexual or romantic context.
To make (someone) feel flushed and hot through drinking alcoholic beverages; also, to make (someone) slightly drunk or tipsy.
ex: His practice of flustering himself daily with claret was hardly considered as a fault by his contemporaries.

s.def: To be agitated and confused; to bustle.

s.def: To become overwhelmed or visibly embarrassed, especially in a sexual or romantic context.

Of a seed: to produce a shoot quickly.
A state of agitation or confusion; a flutter.
A state of slight drunkenness or tipsiness; also, the excitement caused by this state.

ety: From Middle English fleute, floute, flote, from Old French flaute, fleüte, from Old Provençal flaüt, of uncertain origin. Doublet of flauta and fluyt.

An organ stop with a flute-like sound.
A shuttle in weaving tapestry etc.
To play on a flute.

ety: From Middle English floteren, from Old English floterian, flotorian (“to float about, flutter”), from Proto-Germanic *flutrōną, frequentative of Proto-Germanic *flutōną (“to float”), equivalent to float + -er (frequentative suffix). Cognate with West Frisian flodderje (“to flutter, beat”), Dutch flodderen (“to flutter, wave”), Low German fluttern, fluddern (“to flutter”), German flittern (“to sparkle, glitter”). More at float.

To flow as a liquid.

To be distributed in a flowing pattern.

ety: Borrowed from Latin focus (“hearth, fireplace”); see there for more. Related to fuel. Kepler introduced the term into mathematics and the sciences in describing elliptical orbits of planets (quote from Nicholas Mee): "One of the interesting properties of an ellipse is that if there were a light bulb at one focus, then all the light that it emits would reflect off the ellipse and converge at the other focus. This is why Kepler originally used the name focus for these points."

s.def: Concentration of attention.
ex: I believe I can bring the high degree of focus required for this important job.

ex: We self-professed foodies liked to meet in restaurants and talk like experts about what we were eating.

cauterization with electricity; electrocautery

s.def: Containing the maximum possible amount that can fit in the space available.
ex: The jugs were full to the point of overflowing.

s.def: Having the attention, thoughts, etc., absorbed in any matter, and the feelings more or less excited by it.
ex: She's full of her latest project.
Everyone is now full of the miracles done by cold baths on decayed and weak constitutions.

s.def: Complete; with nothing omitted.
ex: Our book gives full treatment to the subject of angling.

s.def: Total, entire.
ex: She had tattoos the full length of her arms. He was prosecuted to the full extent of the law.

ex: full officer

s.def: Having eaten to satisfaction, having a "full" stomach; replete.
ex: "I'm full," he said, pushing back from the table.

s.def: Replete, abounding with.
ex: This movie doesn't make sense; it's full of plot holes.
I prefer my pizzas full of toppings.

s.def: Carrying as much as possible.
ex: Hang on - my hands are full; just let me put these down.

s.def: Plump, round.
ex: full lips; a full face; a full figure

s.def: Having its entire face illuminated.

ety: See Australian slang goog (“egg”).

s.def: Having eaten too much.
ex: ‘I′m full as a goog, Mr Goldberg. Couldn′t manage another crumb.’
After a while I sat back and breathed a heavy sigh. “I am full as a goog!”
‘Don't worry this one′s as full as a goog. It won′t get far,’ Dig yelled, watching the albatross struggle to keep itself aloft.

s.def: Very drunk.
ex: “Well, old Foll was in that bar, as full as a goog.” Mr Jennings leered with the delight that seeing old Foll full as a goog had brought him.
Amos′s grin widened, “You mean the man was drunk?” Mathewson laughed out loud, “He was full as a goog but you said it, laddie, I din′t!”

s.def: A hand that consists of three of a kind and a pair.
ex: This loss of interest, hair, and enterprise — / Ah, if the game were poker, yes, / You might discard them, draw a full house! / But it's chess.

s.def: A situation in which a place is filled with people to its maximum capacity.
A single player scoring a try, conversion, penalty goal and drop goal in the same match
(theater) An event for which every seat is sold out, completely filled with an audience for a play, concert, or movie, creating a successful, packed venue.

ety: From Middle English ful mone, from Old English full mōna, equivalent to full + moon.

s.def: phase of moon when in opposition to sun
The phase of the moon when it is in opposition to the sun and its full disc is therefore visible.
ex: It is true also that the roosters, especially during full moon, crow all night.

s.def: The moon when it is in opposition to the sun.
Egotistical, believing oneself to be superior to others; preoccupied with one's own work, interests, point of view, etc.
Of a window occupying all the available display surface of a screen.
ex: Most computer games are played in full screen mode.

s.def: The punctuation mark ⟨.⟩ (indicating the end of a sentence or marking an abbreviation).
ex: the final period / the final full stop

s.def: A decisive end to something.
A complete stop.
A maximum setting on an engine or motor control: especially, the totally open position of a valve for air intake, but also any corresponding maximum setting.

its regs and serirs over which Land Rovers can race with full throttles and little chance of meeting any obstacle larger than a fist-sized stone.
Under full throttle, your car is just on the border of maximum traction

s.def: A maximum level of speed, effort, or risk.
ex: I'm in the full throttles of an embrace and this is wonderful.
In the third week Dr. Gale shifted into full throttle back pedal.
The full-throttle growth was still in place, as it had been as long as I could remember.

ety: From full + blown, past participle of blow (“to blossom”).

s.def: Completely developed or formed.
ex: We are in the midst of a full-blown crisis.
Solicitor—for just before leaving London I got word that my examination was successful; and I am now a full-blown solicitor!
The Little Ice Age that chilled Europe[…]should, according to past precedents, have snowballed into a full-blown ice age.

s.def: At the peak of blossom; ripe.
ex: The trees in the garden were resplendent with full-blown white gardenias.
Above, Jupiter hung like a full-blown jonquil, so bright as almost to throw a shade.
What made the flower open? What made it grow from a tiny bud to a full-blown bloom? Why was it at all? Why was he?

s.def: Filled with wind; puffed up.
ex: The schooner took to sea with full-blown sails.

ety: From full.

s.def: comparative form of full: more full
ex: Comment must be circumspect until fuller particulars are available, [...].

s.def: One who fulls cloth.
ex: Near-synonyms: feltmaker, felter

s.def: A convex, rounded or grooved tool, used by blacksmiths for shaping metal.
A groove made by such a tool (in the blade of a sword etc.).
To form a groove or channel in, by a fuller or set hammer.
ex: to fuller a bayonet

ety: After Buckminster Fuller, inventor of the geodesic dome, + -ene.

s.def: Any of a class of allotropes of carbon having hollow molecules whose atoms lie at the vertices of a polyhedron having 12 pentagonal and 2 or more hexagonal faces.
Any closed-cage compound having twenty or more carbon atoms consisting entirely of 3-coordinate carbon atoms.
The class of carbon allotropes consisting of tubular carbon molecules (carbon nanotubes) and spheroidal carbon molecules (traditional fullerenes).

ety: From Middle English fulnesse, from Old English fulnes, fylnes, fyllnis (“completeness; abundance”), equivalent to full + -ness. Cognate with Old High German folnissi (“fullness”).

s.def: Being full; completeness.
ex: feel a sense of fullness
The actor enjoyed the fullness of his success.
She lived life in all its fullness.

s.def: The degree to which a space is full.
The degree to which fate has become known.
ex: in the fullness of time
fullness of life

s.def: A measure of the degree to which a muscle has increased in size parallel to the axis of its contraction. A full muscle fills more of the space along the part of the body where it is connected.

ety: From Middle English fully, fulliche, volliche, from Old English fullīċe (“fully”), equivalent to full + -ly. Compare German völlig (“fully”), Swedish fullt (“fully”).

s.def: In a full manner; without lack or defect; completely, entirely.
ex: He is fully capable of meeting his responsibilities.

s.def: Used as an intensifier for a quantity.
ex: it was fully four hours before we arrived home.

s.def: Exactly, equally.
So as to be full (not hungry); to satiation.
ex: to eat fully

s.def: Used as a general intensifier; actually, really, literally.
ex: I fully woke up at like 12 p.m. yesterday.
That is very strange—that is fully my mom.

s.def: To commit or send someone to trial.
ex: So I got run in, and was tried at Marylebone and remanded for a week, and then fullied (fully committed for trial), and got this stretch and a half.

ety: Inherited from Middle English fulminaten, borrowed from Latin fulminātus, perfect passive participle of fulminō (“to lighten, hurl or strike with lightning”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fulmen (“lightning which strikes and sets on fire, thunderbolt”), from earlier *fulgmen, *fulgimen, from fulgeō, fulgō (“flash, lighten”). Doublet of fulmine. More at fulgent.

s.def: To make a verbal attack.
To issue as a denunciation.

To strike with lightning; to cause to explode.

Any salt or ester of fulminic acid, mostly explosive.

ety: From Middle English fulsom, equivalent to full + -some. The meaning has evolved from an original positive connotation "abundant" to a neutral "plump" to a negative "overfed". In modern usage, it can take on any of these inflections. See usage note. The negative sense "offensive, gross; disgusting, sickening" developed secondarily after the 13th century and was influenced by Middle English foul (“foul”). In the 18th century, the word was sometimes even spelled foulsome.

s.def: Offensive to good taste, tactless, overzealous, excessive.
Excessively flattering (connoting insincerity).

s.def: Characterised or marked by fullness; abundant, copious.

s.def: Fully developed; mature.

ety: Borrowed from Latin fulvus (“reddish-brown”).

s.def: Tawny-colored.

The upper wings of the moth which Jacob held were undoubtedly marked with kidney-shaped spots of a fulvous hue.

ety: Borrowed from Italian fumarola. Likely a doublet of femerell. By surface analysis, fume + -ar + -ola.

Of or relating to smoke, smoking, or fumigation.
A place for subjecting things to smoke or vapour.

s.def: To grope awkwardly in trying to find something
ex: He fumbled for his keys.
He fumbled his way to the light-switch.

s.def: To blunder uncertainly.
ex: He fumbled through his prepared speech.

s.def: To grope about in perplexity; to seek awkwardly.

My understanding stutters, and my memory fumbles.

ex: Henderson's best strike on goal saw goalkeeper Kingson uncomfortably fumble his measured shot around the post.

ety: From Middle English fume, from Old French fum (“smoke, steam, vapour”), from Latin fūmus (“vapour, smoke”), from Proto-Indo-European *dʰuh₂mós (“smoke”), from *dʰewh₂- (“to smoke, raise dust”). Doublet of thymus and thymos. More at dun, dusk, dust.

ety: From late Middle English fumyter (with remodelling of suffix), from Old French fumeterre, from Latin fūmus terrae.

ex: This year's fashion style is much more fun than recent seasons.

ety: From French funambule or its source, Latin funambulus, from funis (“rope”) + ambulare (“walk”).

ety: From French fonctionnaire; by surface analysis, function + -ary.

ex: Near-synonyms: bureaucrat; official; officer; administrator; apparatchik

ex: Near-synonyms: bureaucrat, apparatchik; paper-pusher; bean counter

ety: PIE word *bʰudʰmḗn Borrowed from Latin fundus. Doublet of fond and fundus.

a fund for the maintenance of underprivileged students

s.def: A large supply of something to be drawn upon.
ex: He drew on his immense fund of knowledge.
an inexhaustible fund of stories

s.def: To pay or provide money for.
ex: He used his inheritance to fund his gambling addiction.

To form a debt into a stock charged with interest.

ety: From Middle English, from Old French fundement, fondement, from Latin fundāmentum (“foundation”), from fundō (“to lay the bottom, to found”). Doublet of fondamento.

s.def: The underlying basis or principle for a theoretical or mathematical system.
Foundation.
The bottom; the buttocks or anus.
ex: It [the Sphincter Ani] serves to purse up the Fundament, and so hinders the involuntary Evacuation of the Fæces.
I flinched when he touched my rosebud, but pretty soon I was fucking his mouth like it was Hector's fundament.

ety: From Middle English foundamental, fundamental, from Late Latin fundāmentālis, from Latin fundāmentum (“foundation”), from fundō (“to lay the foundation (of something), to found”), from fundus (“bottom”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰmḗn. By surface analysis, fundament + -al.

s.def: any of the fundamental forces that act between elementary particles; each one is associated with an exchanged particle

ety: From fundamental + -ism. First used in the 1910s by American Christians.

s.def: religion
The tendency to reduce a religion to its most fundamental tenets, based on strict interpretation of core texts.
A rigid conformity to any set of basic tenets.
The belief that fundamental financial quantities are the best predictor of the price of a financial instrument.

A Christian movement that started in the late 19th and early 20th centuries among British and American Protestants, which emphasizes literal interpretation of the Bible, and came up as a reaction to liberal theology and cultural modernism

ety: From Latin fūniculus (“thinner cord”), diminutive from fūnis (“rope, cord”) + -culus. By surface analysis, funicul(us) + -ar.

Of or pertaining to the umbilical cord.
Having a fleshy covering of the seed formed from the funiculus, the attachment point of the seed.
Synonym of catenary.

s.def: The act of merging separate things, or the result thereof.
To combine; to fuse.

ety: Of unknown origin. Perhaps from Danish fjas (“nonsense”), from Middle Low German (compare German faseln (“to maunder, talk nonsense”)). Compare also fouse (“to hasten, rush, tumble, disarrange”).

s.def: Excessive activity, worry, bother, or talk about something.
ex: They made a big fuss about the wedding plans.
What's all the fuss about?
Sickness did not last above a ten days; my poor wife zealously assiduous, and with a minimum of fuss or noise.

s.def: A complaint or noise; a scene.
ex: If you make enough of a fuss about the problem, maybe they'll fix it for you.

s.def: An exhibition of affection or admiration.
ex: They made a great fuss over the new baby.

s.def: To be very worried or excited about something, often too much.
ex: His grandmother will never quit fussing over his vegetarianism.

s.def: To fiddle; fidget; wiggle, or adjust
ex: Quit fussing with your hair. It looks fine.

s.def: To disturb (a person)
To cry or be ill-humoured.
To show affection for, especially animals.
To pet.
ex: He fussed the cat.

ety: Etymology tree English fuss Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Germanic *-gaz Proto-West Germanic *-g Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English fussy From fuss + -y.

s.def: Anxious or particular about petty details; hard to please.
Having a tendency to fuss, cry, or be bad-tempered/ill-tempered (especially of babies).
Having much unnecessary detail or decoration.
ex: The internal decor of the SR-built Bulleid corridor stock was noticeably cleaner and less fussy than that of prewar coaches.

ety: Borrowed from Greek φουστανέλα (foustanéla).

s.def: A form of skirt or kilt traditionally worn by men in Albania, Greece and other parts of the Balkans.
ex: The doctor had always wanted a set of fustanella and had never been able to afford it.

ety: The noun is derived from Middle English fustian (“type of fabric, probably made from cotton, flax, or wool; piece of fustian spread over a bed or mattress”) [and other forms], from Old French fustaine, fustaigne (modern French futaine), from Medieval Latin fūstāneum, from (pannus) fūstāneus or (tela) fūstānea, of disputed origin. s.def: Originally, a kind of coarse fabric made from cotton and flax; now, a kind of coarse twilled cotton, or cotton and linen, stuff with a short pile and often dyed a dull colour, which is chiefly prepared for menswear.
A class of fabric including corduroy and velveteen.
Inflated, pompous, or pretentious speech or writing; bombast; also (archaic), incoherent or unintelligible speech or writing; gibberish, nonsense.
Chiefly in rum fustian: a hot drink made of a mixture of alcoholic beverages (as beer, gin, and sherry or white wine) with egg yolk, lemon, and spices.
Made out of fustian (noun sense 1).
ex: His fustian shirt, sanguineflowered, trembles its Spanish tassels at his secrets.

s.def: Of a person, or their speech or writing: using inflated, pompous, or pretentious language; bombastic; grandiloquent; also (obsolete) using incoherent or unintelligible language.
Imaginary; invented.
Useless; worthless.

ety: From Middle English fustik, from Middle French fustec, variant of fustet.

s.def: A tropical American tree (Maclura tinctoria), whose wood produces a yellow dye.
A Eurasian smoketree (Cotinus coggygria), whose wood produces an orange dye.
Wood of these trees.
A yellow dye obtained from the wood of these trees.

ety: First attested in 1656; borrowed from Latin fūstīgātus, perfect passive participle of fūstīgō (“to cudgel to death”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from fūstis (“a cudgel”) + -igō.

s.def: To hit someone with a club.
To harshly criticize someone.

ety: From Middle English fusty, equivalent to fust + -y. Compare Scots foosty.

s.def: Moldy or musty.
Stale-smelling or stuffy.
Old-fashioned, refusing to change or update.
ex: Oh sweet surprise - oh dear delight To find it undisputed quite - All musty, fusty rules despite, That Art is wrong and Nature right!

s.def: Tasting of the cask.
ex: Alison had a mouthful of warm, rather fusty wine and lay back on the grass, cupping the back of her head in her hand.

ety: Borrowed from Middle French futile, from Latin fūtilis.

s.def: Incapable of producing results, useless; doomed not to be successful; not worth attempting.
ex: He seemed hitherto to have been living by proxy, in a vision, in reflection—to have been an echo, a shadow, a futile attempt;[…]
He wished he had not been saddled with Whippham's rather futile son as his chaplain.

s.def: Insignificant; frivolous.
ex: Of its history little is recorded, and that little futile.

ety: Borrowed from Portuguese futsal, a blend of futebol de salão (literally “hall football”).

s.def: A form of soccer played indoors, with five players per team.

ety: From Middle English futtek, votek, of uncertain origin; perhaps a compound of Old English fōt + hōc, or fut + -uc (foot hook or foot -ock), Old Dutch vot or fuot + hoek; or from timber jargon word butt + -ock (diminutive suffix). Alternatively from Middle Dutch voetkijn, diminutive of voet (“foot”), equivalent to foot + -kin; or Old English *fōtuc, meaning foot + -ock (diminutive suffix). Perhaps came into Old English from Old Norse fótr, or fett / futt (big); + ek (timbr), or øks; giving Old N…

s.def: Any of the curved rib-like timbers that form the frame of a wooden ship.

ety: From Middle English future, futur, from Old French futur, from Latin futūrus, irregular future active participle of sum (“to be”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰuH- (“to become, be”). Cognate with Old English bēo (“to become, will be; to be”). More at be. Doublet of futur. Displaced native Old English tōweard, which took on a different meaning as toward, and Middle English afterhede (“future”, literally “afterhood”) in the given sense.

s.def: The time ahead; those moments yet to be experienced.
Something that will happen in moments yet to come.
Goodness in what is yet to come. Something to look forward to.
ex: There is no future in dwelling on the past.

s.def: The likely prospects for or fate of someone or something in time to come.
ex: Again, it's unlikely they will return to traffic, but futures have been secured for four that will be heading to heritage railways [...].

s.def: Verb tense used to talk about events that will happen in the future; future tense.
Alternative form of futures.
An object that retrieves the value of a promise.
A minor-league prospect.
Having to do with or occurring in the future.
ex: Future generations will either laugh or cry at our stupidity.
It[The study] also attempts to predict the future progression of AI as it relates to new inventions.

s.def: The tense or time form of a verb used to refer to an event or occurrence that has not yet happened or is expected to happen in the future.
ex: The future tense came into being as the verbs sculan and willan lost their ancient power as finite verbs and turned into future auxiliaries.

s.def: A standardized contract, traded on a futures exchange, to buy or sell a standardized quantity of a specified commodity (or financial instrument) of standardized quality at a certain date in the future, at a stated price (the futures price).

The Jewish expectation of the messiah in the future.

A future event.
A race for two-year-old horses, nominated to run when still foals.

ety: Uncertain. Some dictionaries suggest a Germanic source; compare Low German fussig (“loose; spongy”), Dutch voos (“unsound; rotten”). Others, such as Webster's New College Dictionary, suggest a back-formation from fuzzy. The Oxford English Dictionary suggests, “Perhaps imitative of the action of blowing away light particles.”

s.def: A frizzy mass of hair or fibre.
ex: His cheeks were like peaches, with much the same sort of fuzz over them.
Once the eaglets are born—tiny balls of white fuzz—the adult eagles prove that birds can be as protective and solicitous of their young as humans.

s.def: Quality of an image that is unclear; a blurred image.
ex: ...scientific advances happen more often at the frontier of representation, at the edge of resolution where an image dissolves into fuzz and blur.

s.def: The random data used in fuzz testing.
ex: "Fuzz testing" or "fuzzing" is a technique for software testing that provides random data ("fuzz") to the inputs of a program.

s.def: A distorted sound, especially from an electric guitar or other amplified instrument.
ex: This gives a good soft clipping effect and a good fuzz sound.

s.def: A state of befuddlement.
ex: So I'm in a fuzz of not knowing what to do

s.def: Fuzziness, vagueness.
To make fuzzy.
To become fuzzy.
To make drunk.
ex: Or maybe my mind was just fuzzed with the drink.

ety: Uncertain. Apparently from fuzz + -y, though some sources suggest that fuzz derives from fuzzy. Compare fozy, or Low German fussig (“loose; spongy”).

Not clear; unfocused.
ex: I finally threw out a large stack of fuzzy photos.

s.def: Vague or imprecise.

Employing or relating to fuzzy logic.
A form of reasoning, derived from fuzzy set theory, whereby a truth value need not be exactly zero (false) or one (true), but rather can be zero, one, or any value in between.

ety: Uncertain, but likely from Middle English fillen (“to fill”) (from Old English fyllan) + fot (“foot”) (from Old English fōt), in reference to its use as a design to be placed at the bottom of stained-glass windows.
